Margaret Rustin BA

Margaret Rustin

Tavistock Clinic

Margaret Rustin   Consultant Child Psychotherapist, Tavistock Clinic, Organizing Tutor of the Tavistock Child Psychotherapy Training, and Dean of Postgraduate Studies at the Tavistock and Portman and N.H.S. Trust

Historical Background

AN UNUSUAL ELEMENT IN THE BRITISH NATIONAL HEALTH SERVICE is that, from its inception, it has encompassed an institution concerned with the development of psychoanalytic psychotherapy; the training of psychotherapists, including a specialized training for child and adolescent psychotherapists; and the broad applications of psychoanalysis to mental health practice, policy, and research. The context in which support for such an institution could be mobilized was the period of post-war reconstruction. Attention had been drawn during the war to the needs of emotionally troubled children. The policies of mass evacuation of children from London had given rise to research and new ideas about the development of children within the family, the crucial role of family relationships, and the pain and damage to personality development attendant on early separation and emotional deprivation. The training in child psychotherapy was created out of John Bowlby's concern that emotionally damaged children should have access to psychotherapeutic treatment.

Prologue

Howard Levine MD Editor and Gail Reed PHD Editor

Gail Reed

Gail Reed  

THIS ISSUE OF PSYCHOANALYTIC INQUIRY is concerned with the problem of compliance in clinical psychoanalysis. To assist us in exploring it, we have asked four prominent analysts of different theoretical orientations—from the British Kleinian (Feldman) to object relations influenced conflict theory (Rizzuto) to social constructivism (Levine) to Self Psychologically influenced intersubjectivist (Lichtenberg)—to illustrate and address how they view and work with compliance in the clinical setting. Their contributions are then discussed by two equally prominent analysts close to the mainstream of contemporary North American psychoanalytic theory and practice (Fogel and Reed).

Compliance is not, of course, a theoretical concept. It is a description of a behavior on a patient's part that impedes the analytic process as that process is seen from the perspective of the practicing analyst. Compliant behavior must consist of clinically manifest action of some kind, yet the criteria for identifying that behavior are variable and unclear. While differences in theoretical perspective may account for some of this variability, agreement on a theoretical perspective does not make it easier to identify clinical criteria.

Within the framework of modern conflict theory, for instance, compliance can be conceptualized as a part of a person's character, to be analyzed when it interferes with adequate functioning, as one would any maladaptive character trait. It can also be seen as a more specific defense appearing at a given moment in an analysis. There the interpretation of the unconscious wish motivating the defense would render it less necessary. Yet even within this agreed upon theoretical framework, neither of these definitions specifies what criteria to use to identify the existence of compliant behavior, let alone the type.

Epilogue

Howard Levine MD Editor and Gail Reed MD Editor

Gail Reed

Gail Reed  

TAKEN AS A WHOLE, the contributions to this issue illustrate the subtlety, pervasiveness, and complexity of the challenge and opportunities presented by the problem of compliance in the analytic clinical setting. As all of our authors have noted, there is a human inevitability to the dialectical tension that exists between those forces that move toward relational cooperation and developmental completion and those that stand in the service of resistance, stasis, avoidance, self-protection, and covert gratification of forbidden desire. Levine and Feldman emphasize that this is as true for the analyst as it is for the patient. (Where they differ is that Feldman takes a somewhat more optimistic stance about the possibility of eliminating such analyst-based, countertransference interference—and in this point he is joined by at least Reed and Fogel—while Levine assumes that some degree of countertransference interference is an inevitable and irreducible aspect of the analyst's subjectivity.)

No matter what their theoretical orientation, however, each of our contributors is sensitively aware that the patient's tendency toward compliance—in its negative sense of a process impeding resistance—becomes most problematic when it elicits or is joined by the analyst's complementary needs to avoid, resist, self-protect, or achieve covert gratification of forbidden desires. Thus, Feldman's focus on the ways in which the analyst may become caught up in compliance with the patient's defensive needs (manifested as compliant behavior within the analysis), leading to a subtle and hard to recognize form of mutual enactment.

By implication, Levine emphasizes the opposite side of the coin when, following on the work of Gill, he discusses the relationship between the analyst's irreducibly suggestive presence and the tendency or pressure for the patient to comply. In his view, the analyst's behavior always reflects some degree of the analyst's defensive needs.

Epilogue

Diana Diamond PHD Editor and Sidney Blatt PHD Editor

Sidney Blatt

Sidney Blatt  

This issue demonstrates that attachment-based theory and research are rapidly expanding the boundaries of psychoanalysis, in both theory and practice. The current engagement of psychoanalysts with attachment research is consistent with the long-standing tradition of integrating child and infant observation and research into psychoanalytic thought. The papers in this issue consider the intersection and divergence between attachment theory and psychoanalysis in an attempt to deepen the dialogue between them. The goal is not to collapse one theory into the other, but to move the discourse into a realm where the essential and irreducible differences between the two traditions are clarified and potential points of contact and overlap are explored, with the view toward developing multidimensional perspectives on theory, research, and clinical practice that encompass both traditions. Indeed, the papers in this issue demonstrate that attachment and psychoanalytic researchers and theorists are still struggling to define their own territory, as well as to identify a common meeting ground. Nonetheless, these papers illustrate that attachment research provides empirically derived data that support important aspects of psychoanalytic theory such as the early developmental antecedents of adult interpersonal relations and the importance of the representational world. A number of papers in this issue call for a reconsideration of psychoanalytic concepts of transference, resistence, motivation, and therapeutic action, as Fonagy, Lichtenberg, and Lyons-Ruth have pointed out. We expect the theoretical debates around these concepts will continue and lead to further discoveries in the laboratory and in the consulting room.

The clinical explorations and concepts of psychoanalysts continue to pose challenges to aspects of attachment theory, just as the research findings of attachment investigators suggest revisions or amplifications of psychoanalytic concepts.

Diana Diamond PHD and Sidney Blatt PHD

Sidney Blatt

Sidney Blatt  

THESE TWO ISSUES DEMONSTRATE that the relationship between attachment theory and psychoanalysis, which began with so much animosity, has evolved into a dialogue of great promise. We can see from these papers that there is an evolving dialectic between attachment theory and psychoanalysis—a dialectic that is moving both traditions forward in a number of directions, both theoretical and clinical, some of which have been addressed in these two issues, some not.

In sum, the seven papers in this volume demostrate the relevance of attachment concepts in clinical work, particularly in understanding aspects of certain clinical disorders, especially dissociative and borderline disorders, and in evaluating and understanding the nature of therapeutic process and change. Further, the papers demostrate that although its use with clinical groups is relatively new, Main and Goldwyn's (1984-1998) system of analyzing a speaker's state of mind with respect to attachment through the AAI has much promise as a research instrument for assessing constructs related to dissociative disorders and borderline disorders, and for empirically investigating therapeutic outcome. Further, these papers contribute to our understanding of the factors that precipitate change in attachment status. Although attachment researchers have demonstrated remarkable predictability in attchment classification, both within the individual over the life cycle and across generations (see Hesse, 1999 for a review), attachment investigators are equally concerned with identifying the discontinuties as well as continuites in attachment organization (Fonagy, 1999; Main, 1999). An indepth examination of particular parent-child dyads with attachment discontinuities (such as that provided by Arietta Slade in this issue) illuminates our understanding of the dynamics underlying discrepancies in attachment status between parent and child.

Parent—Infant Psychotherapy

Remembering the Oedipus Complex

Dilys Daws MA

Dilys Daws

Tavistock Clinic 120 Belsize Lane London NW3 5BA

Dilys Daws   Consultant Child Psychotherapist, Tavistock Clinic, and Chair, AIMH, UK

PARENT–INFANT THERAPY, AND PARTICULARLY BRIEF THERAPY, is, appropriately enough, one of the largest growth areas in psychoanalytic psychotherapy. This work is also perhaps a meeting point with family therapy concepts.

Tom Main, one of the British “Independents,” said of psychoanalysis that sitting behind a couch five times a week was only one of its applications. With that definition in mind, one need not be shy of thinking of the dramatic and eventful meetings with parents and their infants as equally one of its applications.

At the Tavistock Clinic, a flourishing Under Five's Counselling Service offers brief work with families of infants. I am a part of this service and also work at a baby clinic in a general medical practice in a local health center, alongside the family doctors and “health visitors” who are nurses with special training to support young families.

At both places I see families about difficulties in their infant's development. Many cases are referred as sleeping or feeding problems or excessive crying; in addition, some parents will come, openly talking about their difficulty in “bonding,” in making a relationship with their baby, and now that postnatal depression is so much more easily recognized, many mothers come for help about their state of mind and its effect on their relationship with their baby. With older babies and toddlers, another range of problems are presented: those of weaning and separation difficulties, toilet training, and behavior problems.

Introduction

Thou Cams't on earth to make the earth my hell

A grievous burden was thy birth to me.

Tetchy and wayward was thy infancy

Thy schooldays frightful, desp'rate, wild and furious …

“The Ghost of an Idea….”

On Scrooge, Internal Worlds and Attachment Patterns

Janet Philps D.Phil.

Janet Philps

Tavistock Clinic
120 Belsize Lane
London NW3 5BA

Janet Philps   Child and Adolescent Psychotherapist, Outpatient Clinics, Stevenage and Milton Keynes, and Visiting Teacher, Tavistock Clinic

IN THE ALLEGORY OF SCROOGE'S CONVERSION, Dickens' appeal, written in what were called the “Hungry Forties,” was to the “Ghost of an Idea”: of a crisis of conscience in “the selfishness and indifference of the prosperous classes, who parrot phrases about the surplus population and assume their social responsibilities to be fully discharged when they paid their taxes.” It is the reader's social conscience and charitable feelings that Dickens urgently and deeply touches. “The shame and horror of desperate poverty and the danger to society” that is represented by the apparitions of future “Ignorance and Want” impress upon us the very urgent social need for Scrooge's change of heart and mind (Slater, 1971, in Dickens, 1843). His success in this is tremendously relieving to the reader.

From a child psychotherapy and developmental psychology perspective, however, my aim is to think about Scrooge less as social allegory and more in terms of what Dickens allows us to understand about him as a family member, as an individual with an emotional life. His apparent selfishness and indifference seem closely bound up with his own emotional ignorance and want, which Dickens explores in terms of his emotionally deprived relationships in the past and his self-imposed isolation in the present.

This paper is revised and much abridged from a Christmas lecture given in December 1996, when I was asked to describe the kind of work I do as a child psychotherapist, to an audience of social workers, health visitors, and counsellors.

Elizabeth Carr RNCS MSN Editor

Elizabeth Carr

Elizabeth Carr  

IN WRITING THIS EPILOGUE, I find myself wearing two hats: first, as a clinician who is reporting her work during the early phase of analytic therapy with a very challenging patient. I begin by expressing my gratitude to Aaron. I have learned a great deal from my collaboration with him during our journey of exploration and making sense of his and our experience. From a difficult beginning, our work has become richer and remains both challenging and stimulating, facilitating my own growth as an analyst. In the clinical presentation describing our work together, I wrote about how “daunting” I found it at the beginning because of Aaron's long history of failed treatment. My anxiety was exacerbated by my own insecurity as I compared my skills with those of the revered “senior analyst” who had referred Aaron to me. In the paper, I described my own sense of anticipatory shame as I wondered if I would be up to the task of helping Aaron. As you may expect, that sense of being anxiously challenged pales in contrast to having my work discussed by six shame experts. Providing a clinical presentation, “warts and all,” and having it discussed is somewhat a humbling experience. In some instances, I look back and wish that I had responded differently at particular moments. For example, I agree that I added to Aaron's shame during the padded-cell sequence when I asked where I was in his fantasy. At that moment, my own countertransference anxiety and uncertainty interfered with my understanding of Aaron's need to stay hidden and disconnected. Overall, however, I am gratified to have my work taken seriously by the discussants and to hear their reactions to it. I personally have learned from their comments. I am also pleased that my openness in providing case material has contributed to a fuller understanding of different theoretical views of shame and their therapeutic implications.

My second hat is as editor of this issue on shame and self disorders. Here, I am extremely grateful to all the contributors for their illuminating and thoughtful exploration of these topics.

EACH PSYCHOANALYTIC THEORY OF THE DEVELOPMENT and the workings of the psyche is most convincing at the point of its central thesis and less salient when issues that lie outside its main premise are being considered. Attachment theory's central premise is that infants organize demonstrable patterns of behavior and internal working models in response to the need for a secure base in times of danger and loss. Other psychoanalytic theories have confirmed their central hypothesis. Freud convincingly demonstrated infantile sexuality and the oedipal complex. The existence of important pregenital forces have been substantiated, although with differing emphases by Mahler, object relationists, Klein, and Kohut. None of the other theories have presented more careful observation and research to establish its central premise than attachment. Establishing the three categories (Ainsworth) and the fourth (Main) across the world is a scientific tour de force. The second finding, that the categories have statistically significant predictability over time, adds powerful confirmation. At this point in its development, attachment's secure base hypothesis rests somewhere between a proven pattern of behavior and a more process-organized internal working model or models of attachment responses. The Adult Attachment Interview (AAI) permitted a further discovery of an unexpected strong relation between modes of communication about attachment experiences by an adult, the attachment patterns that adult had as a 1-year old, and the likely attachment pattern of children that that adult will parent.

MOST HUMAN ACTIONS INVOLVE AN ELEMENT of compliance. The social framework of human life, the interpersonal nature of human activities in reality and fantasy, and the developmental formation of the psyche in the context of human relational exchanges make compliance with the real or assumed wishes of another an essential and unavoidable component of the psyche itself. Without compliance there is no psychic life. This proposition calls for a clarification of the concept of compliance in its semantic and psychic meanings. The term comply appears in English and in the romance languages from about 1600 as a derivative of the Latin complire, to fulfill, complete. The evolution of meaning brought it to the realm of interpersonal courtesy. Further semantic transformation carried the term to its present-day prevalent meaning: “To comply with a person's desires, requests, requirements, conditions, etc.” (Compact Oxford English Dictionary, 1971). Webster's New Universal Unabridged Dictionary (1979) gives the word a less interpersonal definition: “To yield in compliance; to act in accordance with a request, demand, order, rule” while keeping its social value, “to be formally polite.”

The semantic exploration of the term points to the meaning bridging the original sense of completing something in itself to the social and interpersonal acts of acquiescing to rules and desires of another.

A unique feature of analysis is that the shifting strains at the junction of the analysand's and analyst's activities create a relational exchange, one that calls for definition and a comprehensible set of emotion-laden meanings. Thus, the relationship between analyst and analysand provides more than the working basis for the analysis; its shifting strains provide crucial data, from which the most significant aspects of understanding are derived [Lichtenberg, 1983, pp. 236-237).

The analysand will be under all the strains and tensions brought to the analysis as a consequence of the full accumulation of unresolved regulatory disturbances and conflicts from the past. In the analysis, the analysand will be pulled toward an internally obligatory (and analytically necessary) full expression of his or her perceived needs and wishes—as an immediate demand. At the same time the analysand will be drawn by the desire to comply with the goal shared with the analyst, to confined action and interaction to exploring meanings [Lichtenberg, 1983, p. 235].

ONE OF THE LABORS OF HERCULES was to wrestle with Proteus, the monster who kept changing shapes from serpent to lion to bear. Hercules managed to hang on and hold the monster despite the transformations. Those who would write about shame are in a similar predicament: they must hang on despite the anxiety over metamorphoses. Attempting to grasp shame in the consulting room is very much like wrestling with Proteus: it keeps changing shapes. Elizabeth Carr struggles valiantly to hang onto the subject of shame and thereby provides us with an opportunity to consider her process notes. Mine is only one reading of the paper she has generously provided, which, I hope, will be complemented by other readings in this issue.

In the first part of this paper, I will focus on the clinical picture and on a few of the clinical interactions that can be used to illustrate shame manifestations in the transference and countertransference. In the second part, I will discuss these shame manifestations freely with respect to literary and philosophical examples.

The question of the centrality of shame in the disorders of the self can be approached in many ways. I hope to be able to show that one does not necessarily have to subscribe to a particular view of the disorders of the self in order to view shame as extremely useful clinically.

THERE IS, IN ORDINARY USAGE AS WELL AS IN PSYCHOANALYSIS, a wonderful ambiguity about the word compliance. The term has been used to embrace a wide concept of accord. “He [Paul] tells them of his tears, and they answer him with tears: O happy compliance!” (Trapp, 1656).

Its more modern use involves the individual's acting in accordance with, or yielding to a “desire, request, condition, direction, etc.” (Oxford English Dictionary, 1989). However, the O.E.D. clearly recognizes the variety of motives, and degrees of coercion involved. Thus compliance may be freely and gladly achieved or demanded by a powerful figure, under threat. Burnet (1699) describes a situation in which “it was only a Compliance, and not a Submission to their opinions, that … (made them observe certain practices).” Phillips (1863) suggests that “all politics necessitates questionable compliances.”

These issues will be familiar in the analytic dialogue. The patient feels a degree of compliance is required of him—both in relation to the analytic setting and the “desire, request, condition, direction, etc.” he feels implicit in the analyst's verbal interventions. The requirement or pressure for compliance is felt to be a potent force and invokes infantile, childhood, and adolescent struggles with external and internal demands and the accommodations that were arrived at. It is never simple but usually involves some combination of willing agreement and conscious or unconscious submission—out of a desire to defer to powerful authority, out of fear, or for masochistic reasons.

THIS PAPER IS WRITTEN IN RESPONSE to Carr's request that I consider the question, “Is shame the central affect in disorders of the self?” and that I comment on her paper, “Wounded But Still Walking: One Man's Effort to Move Out of shame.”

The central question of this issue and Carr's presentation is posed by a colleague whose clinical work is organized from the theoretical perspective of an evolved self psychology. I, in contrast, experience my clinical work from the perspective of an evolved Freudian theory: Compromise Formation Theory.

From the perspective of self psychology, as Kohut (1977), Broucek (1982, 1991), and Morrison (1983) have emphasized, shame is the central affect of self psychology. Patients are thought to be afflicted with “disorders of the self.” Because I work from a different theoretical perspective, I think about the people I collaborate with in analytic work and our affects in a different way.

In pursuit of the goal of this paper, a review of the history of psychoanalytic ideas on shame is presented to contribute to answering the central question of this issue, “Is shame the central affect in disorders of the self?” My own understanding of shame is presented as part of that review. Then I will comment on Carr's work with Aaron from the perspective of my thinking about affects.

IN THIS PAPER ON INTROJECTIVE PROCESSES, I am mainly relying on a Kleinian frame of reference and some concepts of Bion. Nevertheless, if I try to describe the central theme, I cannot think of a more beautiful image than the one provided by Freud (1917) when he spoke, in “Mourning and Melancholia” of the “shadow of the object falling upon the ego” and of the paraphrases of this sentence offered by Karl Abraham (1924) when speaking of the “radiance of the object” reflected upon the ego.

This play of lights and shadows in the quality of the internal objects acquires an almost tangible dimension in the description of the internal world and of the internal space that is central in the work of Klein. The existence of this internal space was implicitly present in the work of Freud: he spoke about the shadow of the object; this internal object must occupy an internal space. In the case of Schreiber, Freud (1911) spoke of the external catastrophe being a mirror image of an internal catastrophe.

I shall begin with a description of introjective processes that is more related to the play of lights than to the play of shadows. I wish to talk, first of all, of introjective processes that facilitate development. In the second part of this paper, I will focus on particular types of introjective processes that create an obstacle to development and may bring about the introjection of an object performing a function that is the obverse of alpha function.

BABIES HAVE IMMENSE MEANING for their parents. They are the object of wishes and dreams: through the baby, parents hope to perpetuate the best of themselves and to fulfill what has remained unrealized in their own lives. Babies can also be the recipients of what is most painfully secret in the parents' psyches. When this happens, babies become the carriers of the parents' unconscious fears, impulses, and other repressed or disowned parts of themselves.

This paper focuses on a particular aspect of this phenomenon: how mothers make negative attributions on their young children and how those negative attributions are internalized by the child and become an integral part of the child's sense of self. This intimate process of communication between mother and infant represents a particularly rich area for dialogue between attachment theory and psychoanalysis. This paper has three major goals in striving toward an integration of these two theoretical approaches. One goal is to highlight the contributions of attachment theory to clinical practice through an increasing recognition of the pivotal importance of real-life events, including actual interactions with the mother, in molding the child's inner world and sense of self. A second goal is to underline the clinical relevance of the protective function served by the attachment bond.

IT IS GENERALLY ACCEPTED BY PSYCHOANALYSTS that there is something wrong with attachment theory. Opposition to attachment theory for once united the warring factions of the British Psycho-Analytical Society (the Anna Freudians and the Kleinians) (Grosskruth, 1986). Many major figures contributed to this one-sided debate between psychoanalysis and attachment theory (e.g., Engel, 1971; Rochlin, 1971; Kernberg, 1976a; Roiphe, 1976; Hanly, 1978).

A film called Assault on Precinct 13 begins with a sequence of shots of a gang of young men riding around the Watts District of Los Angeles in a car, aiming rifles first at an old black woman, then at a white man, then at a black man. Their fun is at least racially undiscriminating. The aiming seems random, idle, almost whimsical. We get to see the quarry lined up in the sights of the rifle each time, but noone pulls the trigger. The members of the gang seem to be having a good time. (Bruce Chatwin [1987] observed that, in the language of many nomadic peoples, the word for townspeople is “meat.”) The scene then switches to a little girl buying an ice cream from an ice cream vendor while her father makes a phone call from a call box. She returns to her father but suddenly looks at her ice cream with dismay and turns back to the ice cream van. She does not realize that by then the gang has killed the ice cream vendor, and the man standing in the van is his killer. She says, “Excuse me, I asked for chocolate and you've given me strawberry!” The killer turns and, as casually as he might swat a fly, shoots her in her still open mouth. It is horrifying, and what is particularly horrifying about it is the casualness. The killer does not appear to be angry, nor does he give any sign of sadistic relish. He looks at most mildly irritated.

THEORETICAL EMPHASES IN PSYCHOANALYSIS HAVE CHANGED over the years from classical drive theory to an increasing focus on the role of object relationships and object representation in personality development and psychopathology (e.g., Winnicott, 1960; Blatt, 1974; Mahler, Pine, and Bergman, 1975; Kernberg, 1976; Blatt & Lerner, 1983a). Central to object relational models is the concept of mental representation of self and other. Mental representations are enduring cognitive-affective psychological structures that provide templates for processing and organizing information so that new experiences are assimilated to existing metal structures. These mental schemas guide an individual's behavior, particularly in interpersonal relationships (Blatt & Lerner, 1983b). These cognitive-affective schemas or mental representations of self and other develop over the life cycle. They have conscious and unconscious cognitive, affective, and experiential components that derive from significant early interpersonal experiences.

THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN PSYCHOLOGICAL TRAUMA AND DISSOCIATIVE processes is established on firm empirical grounds (Van der Kolk, 1987; Spiegel, 1991; Herman, 1992; Warshaw et al., 1993; Marmar et al., 1994). In many clinical and epidemiological studies, patients likely to suffer from dissociative mental states—not only those diagnosed within the category of the dissociative disorders, but also many of those suffering from eating disorders and borderline personality disorders—have reported memories of childhood sexual, physical, or emotional abuses (Kluft, 1985; Bliss, 1986; Herman, Perry, and Van der Kolk, 1989; Putnam, 1989; Ross, 1989; Palmer et al., 1990; Strick and Wilcoxon, 1991; Waller, 1991; Gunderson and Sabo, 1993; Van der Linden, 1993; Everill and Waller, 1995; Dalle Grave et al., 1996). Because of the relationship between traumatic experiences in childhood and development of these disorders in adult life, both dissociative disorder and borderline personality disorder have been regarded as forms of chronic post-traumatic stress disorder (Ross, 1989; Gunderson and Sabo, 1993). Measures of dissociative experiences (such as the Dissociative Experience Scale [DES]: Bernstein and Putnam, 1986) have shown, in these diagnostic categories, how often and how tightly dissociation is linked to traumatic memories (for a review, see Van IJzendoorn and Schuengel, in press).

How Attachment Theory Can Contribute to the Understanding of Affective Functioning in Psychoanalysis

Massimo Ammaniti MD

Massimo Ammaniti

Via dei Marsi 78, Rome, Italy 00185

Massimo Ammaniti   Psychoanalyst and Professor of Developmental Psychopathology. University of Rome “La Sapienza.”

THIS PAPER BRIEFLY REVIEWS THE MOST RELEVANT psychoanalytic theories about affect, which still have a questionable status, as Shapiro and Emde (1992) have recently emphasized. Attachment theory, since Bowlby's early papers, stresses the affective bond between infant and caregiver. According to different strategies of attachment (secure, avoidant, ambivalent), emotional experience and regulation are discussed. From infancy to adulthood emotions are intertwined with representations of self and attachment figures (internal working model). In this context, affects are no more considered “drive derivatives,” but they create an “affective communication system” (Tronick, 1989), in which the infant and adults are participants.

With these perspectives a vignette is presented about clinical observations of a young man who suffers from substance dependence and mood disorder. In particular, considering the narrative structure of the patient's communication, the attachment strategies are investigated.

In the concluding remarks it is suggested that mental representations of attachment could be conceived of as a network whose different attachment strategies could be activated by the interaction with others.

Melvin Lansky   Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, UCLA Medical School, and Training and Supervising Analyst, Los Angeles Psychoanalytic Institute

I

SHAME IS ABOUT THE SELF. The word as we now understand it refers, not simply to one type of affect, but to a complex emotional system regulating the social bond, that is, signaling disturbance to the status of the self within the social order: what one is before oneself and others; one's standing, importance, or lack of it; one's lovability, sense of acceptability, or imminent rejection, as seen before the eye of the other or the internal self-evaluative eye of the self. This essential relationship to the self is in contrast to the domain of guilt, which does not concern the self—what one is—so much as it does what one does—real or fantasied actions, transgressions, or omissions that harm the other.

I shall trace some of the details of this linkage of shame and the self and also the evolving understanding of the phenomenology of shame and of the relation of this to the understanding of the centrality of self-experience to a wide range of disturbances that we may call disorders of the self.

I shall nonetheless contend that seeing shame as the central affect of disorders of the self is highly problematic and involves a conceptual error that, if it holds us captive, risks impeding our understanding of the phenomenology of shame, of the psychopathology of self disorders, and of the significance of psychodynamics generally.

ANSWERING THE TITLE QUESTION of this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry (Is shame the central affect of disorders of the self?) seems intuitively straightforward: Yes, shame is the central affect for disorders of the self. Elizabeth Carr's case provides us with a wealth of clinical material with which to examine the question, although I am unable to examine the separate topics of shame, affect, and disorders of the self as fully as they deserve. I hope the reader will accept the speculative spirit in which I offer my ideas about the title question and the case material.

But perhaps the question itself deserves closer examination before we answer it so easily. To begin, I find it useful to understand shame, not as an affect, but as an emotion. Most writers who consider shame an innate affect cite Tomkins (1962, 1963), who defined shame-humiliation as an affect auxiliary, meaning that it functioned as a “specific inhibitor of continuing interest and enjoyment” (1963, p. 123).1 Shame-humiliation consists of an innate reaction that functions primarily to reduce facial communication, and includes lowered eyes, dropped head, and blushing. IN MANY FIELDS, A TENSION EXISTS between researchers and practitioners, the practitioners contemptuously labeling the researchers as bean counters and the researchers returning the compliment in referring to practitioners as too unintellectual to appreciate the purity of science. For many years within psychoanalysis the tilt was so great that little reputable research existed outside the clinical endeavor. The core object of psychoanalytic study, the unconscious, was reachable only in transference-driven dreams and associations kept uncontaminated by the analyst's neutrality and abstinence. With a shift from an almost exclusive focus on unconscious fantasy to object relations and intersubjectivity, the object of study shifted to aspects of self with other and transference—countertransference transactions opening the way to limited statistical research within the field (Luborsky and Crits-Christoph, 1989; Weiss and Sampson, 1986) using data of the consulting room. In the meantime a large body of observational, experimental, and statistical research was taking place outside the consulting room. I have summarized much of this research (Lichtenberg, 1983, 1985) and its relationship to psychoanalysis. This volume and the one that precedes it draw on another now vast complex body of research derived from Bowlby's concept of attachment. Until very recently, psychoanalysts, with a few exceptions, have been reluctant to draw on this potentially valuable source of information. While a wave of interest has risen, tensions exist between the two fields that create a border area for creative exploration.

CONFUSION ABOUT THE MEANING OF CONCEPTS is one of the most common causes of disagreement in psychoanalytic debate and is especially striking when affects are the topic of discussion. In commenting on these discussions by seven experts on shame, then, clarification of the meaning of shame and related terms will be my first focus. After such clarification, I will try to synthesize a rather comprehensive model of that affect. I will then turn to the question that is the focus of this issue: “Is shame the central affect in disorders of the self?” Since all psychoanalytic theorists are clinicians first, much of the theoretical discussion herein is, as it should be, in terms of the clinical material that has been presented. I will conclude by trying to pull together some of these clinical ideas about Aaron specifically and, more generally, about some technical approaches to the sometimes difficult problem of treating patients with intense shame.

Problems in Defining Shame

Hamish Canham   is Child Psychotherapist, Child and Family Department, Tavistock Clinic

I HAVE NOTICED REPEATEDLY DISTORTIONS in the perception of time in fostered and adopted children: a 6-year-old girl in foster care who had no idea of what day of the week it was, a 12-year-old adopted girl who did not know how old she was or what time of the day it was, a 12-year-old fostered boy who could not tell the time, and a 15-year-old boy in therapy for a year who thought his sessions lasted for an hour and a half.

These difficulties with time are also apparent in an often confused sense of past, present, and future, where past experiences remain undifferentiated from the present and where an idea of the future is of something just like the past.

The consistency with which I have encountered this kind of phenomena has led me to question why the various experiences of fostered and adopted children have given rise to these distortions in the perception of time. In this paper, I want to look at some of the ways these distortions take place and how psychoanalytic psychotherapy can help deal with these difficulties.

It should be clear that, when I refer to the concept of time, I do not simply mean an ability to grasp chronological time as measured in minutes, hours, days, weeks, and so on, but also a sense of past, present, future; of order and sequence; of development; and of causality.

RECENT PSYCHOANALYTIC THEORY HAS MOVED INCREASINGLY toward a relational, intersubjective, and social—constructivist stance. In this view the psychoanalytic encounter is seen as mutually coconstructed between two active participants, with the subjectivities of both patient and analyst contributing to the form and content of the dialogue that emerges between them (McLaughlin, 1991; Hoffman, 1992; Ogden, 1994). The current emphasis in analytic writing on the importance of enactments in the treatment situation attempts to keep the lens focused squarely on the point of contact between the two analytic participants and on the form of the implicit transactions that emerge between them (e.g., Ogden, 1994). Clinical descriptions acknowledge the active contributions of both partners to the co-construction of the enactment, even though the primary clinical interest may be in those features of the enactment that echo problematic aspects of the patient's interactions with other important people (Jacobs, 1991; Hoffman, 1992).

WE HAVE JUST READ A VERY CONVINCING DESCRIPTION of a case of a man in whom the various aspects of shame played symptomatically and phenomenologically a crucial role. For Aaron, as for so many other patients who are filled with symptomatic shame, the answer to our issue's question “Is shame the central affect of disorders of the self?” has to be yes. Disturbances of self-esteem, of self-respect, of self-cohesion and the sense of integrity—in brief, of narcissism in the widest sense—all these terms describe a set of problems we encounter in most of our patients, and with that we also encounter with great prominence the affect and the state of shame, the anxiety of shame, and the protective attitude of shame.

PICTURE AARON: 45 YEARS OLD; sturdy; stocky; alone on a bleak, burnt-out landscape; his right foot injured; blood oozing from his wounds; his face controted with pain. Still on his feet, Aaron drags himself forward—slowly, laboriously, but always moving in a forward direction. In this paper I will tell the story of my work with Aaron, slowly moving forward over the past two and a half years.

Shame is at the very center of Aaron's self-experience. His sense of himself as rotten to the core and totally undeserving permeates every moment of his empty, miserable existence. There is little pleasure or satisfaction in his life. And although he longs to feel differently—to feel confident, to life himself, and to enjoy intimacy with others— Aaron finds that he is helplessly locked into the worst kind of human suffering: the suffering of unremitting self-loathing.

I should also mention that Aaron is very intelligent and can show a wry sense of humor. He has overcome a number of adversities to marry, complete a graduate program, and function effectively in a well-paid professional job. Despite considerable innate strengths and talents, Aaron is hobbled by the feelings of shame within him. My paper will describe how we have understood and worked with these particular problems.

IN THE “TRADITIONAL CLASSICAL” VIEW of the analytic process (Levine, 1994), analysts were seen as objective observers who, given their capacity to hold their countertransference in check, could interpret from a stance that was more or less abstinent and neutral. According to this formulation, under these “good enough” analytic conditions, transference was something that pertained to the patient, technically correct interpretations were considered to be rationally based conveyors of verbal content, rather than forms of action or impulse and meaning and memory,1 while not invariably so, were more or less viewed as objective and stable. The stance of objectivity and neutrality to which analysts aspired insured that suggestion could be minimized, if not eliminated, by a combination of the analyst's technical intent and personal preparation (i.e., analysis and self-analysis). Under such conditions, compliance was seen as a reflection of the patient's conflicts, wishes, and defensive needs.

1As I have noted elsewhere (Levine, 1993), the constructivist view of memory as mutable and context dependent has roots in Freud's (1899) early paper “Screen Memories,” in which he wrote: “It may indeed be questioned whether we have any memories at all from childhood: memories relating to our childhood may be all that we possess. Our childhood memories show us our earliest years not as they were but as they appeared at the later periods when the memories were aroused. In these periods of arousal, the childhood memories did not, as people are accustomed to say, emerge; they were formed at that time. And a number of motives, with no concern for historical accuracy had a part in forming them, as well as in the selection of the memories themselves.” (p. 322). This is in contrast to Freud's (e.g., 1937) more usual discussion of memory as archeological find.40

BY THIS POINT IN THE JOURNAL readers will have obtained a detailed and varied knowledge about shame. First, Aaron's version cannot fail to move us to sympathy for his lifelong suffering and prior treatment failures. Second, Carr's openness has allowed us to share her experience and compare our own theories and clinical approaches. Then we hear from a group of analysts who, starting 2 decades ago with Wurmser, are responsible for the current upsurge of interest, and others, Malin and Rothstein, whose contributions are more recent. Included in their essays are reviews of the history of the concept of shame from Freud to the present, with special emphasis on the distinction between shame and guilt. The contributions of Piers and Singer, Tomkins, Kohut, Broucek, H. B. Lewis, and M. Lewis are noted. And without undue labeling, theories of ego psychology, Klein, self psychology, and Brenner are applied to the clinical material. So what remains for a commentator is to wrestle with the different positions and offer or burden readers with yet another view.

Before doing so, I believe it is only fair to confirm what many readers may have surmised. I do not come at either the question about centrality or the case material at a “neutral” distance.

THERE IS A TRADITION IN PSYCHOANALYSIS of revisiting old concepts in the light of new theoretical developments. The authors who contribute to this special issue on changing notions of the compliant patient represent a range of important points of view in our contemporary pluralistic psychoanalytic climate—ego-psychological, object-relational, and self-psychological. Their ideas arise at a time of paradigm shift in psychoanalysis. Where once we assumed we could view the patient objectively or through a neutral lens, we now mostly agree that the analyst's subjectivity is inevitable—that both analyst and patient are participant observers in an intersubjective and interpersonal field. Additionally, in clinical analysis there are two persons mutually affecting and influencing each other, reflecting an underlying two-person rather than a one-person psychological field. Every author reflects this conceptual shift to a greater or lesser extent. All, for example, routinely reveal their personal thoughts and feelings, and utilize these to discern what is happening in the analytic process.

But despite this shared context, I cannot discern that clear themes or lines of convergence and divergence arise from this collection of articles. Synthesis does not seem possible. Each contributor has a piece of the elephant and I cannot make out the whole.

THE TAVISTOCK CLINIC, AN EXCITING PLACE, was founded in 1920 and has always had a community mental health purpose. Its child psychotherapy training began just 50 years ago, in 1948, organized by John Bowlby, then Chairman of the Children's Department, and with the inspiration of Esther Bick.

Anna Freud had started the Hampstead Child Therapy Course the previous year in 1947, and both had been preceded by Margaret Lowenfeld who pioneered a small training in 1933. This later became the Institute of Child Psychology, which closed 20 years ago.

The overall professional body, the Association of Child Psychotherapists (ACP), was established in 1949. There are now six training schools answerable to it. As well as the Tavistock Clinic and the Anna Freud Centre, there are ones within the British Association of Psychotherapists and the Society of Analytical Psychologists (Jungian), two trainings more recently set up outside London, the Birmingham Training in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy and one at the Scottish Institute of Human Relations in Edinburgh and Glasgow.

Child psychotherapy is flourishing in the UK, mainly within the National Health Service (NHS), itself founded in 1948. The NHS, with free healthcare accessible to all, is one of the great achievements of this country. Mary Boston and I wrote about an earlier stage of development of the profession (Daws and Boston, 1977), and a forthcoming book by Horne and Lanyado (1999) will mark the 50th Anniversary of the ACP.

Child psychotherapists work in Child and Family Consultation Centres in the community; they also work in hospital psychiatric and pediatric departments, in social services, and increasingly with GPs, that is, family doctors.

THIS PAPER DESCRIBES THE DEVELOPMENT and gradual dissolution of narcissistic illusions, characterized by idealization, grandiosity and merger, in the psychotherapy of an 18-year-old girl.

Two different traditions regarding the understanding and treatment of narcissism originated in London. Klein and her followers (notably Kernberg) have emphasized the need to interpret these illusions as defensive retreats from acute ambivalence, while Winnicott considered that they represented developmental opportunities. This paper shows how there is value in both these approaches and suggests that more attention should be given to the wider role of object-relationships in the development of narcissism, a view supported by attachment theory.

Referral and Background

Roberta was the second of three daughters born to parents who were national celebrities in the world of television. She sought help for depression and for a distressing feeling that she could never be satisfied. I found her to be a beautiful, vivacious adolescent of 18, fashionably and seductively dressed.

OVER THE LAST 30 YEARS there has been a resurgence of interest and thoughtful scholarship within the psychoanalytic community concerning shame affects and the concepts of self and self disorders. This has in many ways altered the psychoanalytic landscape and influenced both discourse on theory and clinical practice. This issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry continues this tradition and hopes to expand understanding of shame and disorders of the self, as well as to explore the convergence of the two topics.

This issue had its genesis at a conference held in Washington, DC, which had as its topic Is Shame the Central Affect in Disorders of the Self? The conference was sponsored by the Institute of Contemporary Psychotherapy, a professional organization with a focus on self psychology and other contemporary models of psychoanalytic therapy. The goal of the meeting was to bring together experts in the field of shame to address the question, from their particular theoretical perspective and from the perspective of a case presentation. At that conference I gave the clinical presentation, a version of which is included in this issue. Leon Wurmser and Andrew Morrison served as discussants. The conference was greeted enthusiastically and generated a lively exchange of ideas. Following this, an expanded discussion of this topic in an issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry seemed a very good idea. We have been very fortunate to add to the list of shame experts the names of Arnold Rothstein, Melvin Lansky, Benjamin Kilborne, and Barnet Malin. Each provided a discussion of the question posed in this issue as it related to the case material and to their theoretical and clinical positions. After these discussions, Sydney Pulver and Joe Lichtenberg agreed to review the clinical presentation and the papers by the shame experts and provide a synthesis and discussion of the question raised in this issue.

I present the case of Aaron, a man who comes to psychoanalytic therapy with an overwhelming sense of personal shame and misery.

Joseph Lichtenberg MD Editor

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg  

THESE TWO VOLUMES on attachment theory and research are dedicated to the memory of Mary D. Saltar Ainsworth, who died on March 21, 1999.

Mary Saltar Ainsworth, as I think of her over our 40 years of acquaintance, was large—large physically, large in heart, and very, very large in accomplishment. The theory of attachment we document in these two volumes of Psychoanalytic Inquiry could not have come about without her brilliance and simplicity, a rare combination. If Mary wanted to see if Bowlby's ideas were correct, she went where she could observe the evidence. Observing, for Mary, meant looking with the most sensitive powers of perception at the whole of child rearing in Uganda. Simplicity meant that if she wanted to observe responses to separation in an urban culture, she would set up a test situation that could be standardized and confirmed by others. Look, study, document—not coldly, not experience distant, but right where we live as humans. Thus Mary chose for her book Infancy in Uganda the subtitle Infant Care and the Growth of Love. Mary's writing reveals her freedom from the distraction of all the psychoanalytic arguments about drive theory that swirled around Bowlby. She simply went to the heart of the matter—the caregiver and the child and their interplay. We psychoanalysts now reap the harvest of her freedom to explore. In an inscription to the Uganda book Mary gave me on its publication, she wrote: “I hope you enjoy this. I enjoyed writing it.” Mary knew how to enjoy—to play. We lose her in death but, as she taught us, attachment is about the mastery of danger and loss.

WE ARE AT A PRIVILEGED MOMENT in the study of the relationship between attachment theory and psychoanalysis. Psychoanalysis has always had close links to developmental psychology, being enriched by development theory and research and, in turn, contributing to and participating in developmental investigations. This close relationship between attachment and developmental psychology has been enriched and extended over the past two decades by the identification of several different patterns of attachment between infant and the caregiver (Ainsworth et al., 1978) and of the representational processes that are the “likely mediators of differences in parental caregiving” (Hesse, 1999, p. 395; Main, Kaplan, and Cassidy, 1985). Attachment theory and research initially emerged from the clinical observations of the psychoanalyst John Bowlby, who identified the proclivity to form affectional bonds with significant others who are likely to promote the individual's safety and survival as pivotal to human motivation. He theorized that this affectional bond serves the evolutionary function of maintaining the infant's proximity to the mother in the face of separation, and that the child will inevitably develop strategies to regulate proximity to the caretaker, strategies shaped in part by the nature of the caretaker's response to the child's distress at separation and attempts to reestablish proximity (Bowlby, 1969, 1973, 1988). Bowlby's delineation of the attachment motivational system was enhanced and extended through considerable experimental investigation, first by Mary Ainsworth (Ainsworth et al., 1978, 1985) and later by a host of other investigators, some of whom have contributed to this two-issue series on psychoanalysis and attachment theory and research. Most readers of this prologue are already familiar with the basic tenets of attachment theory and research, but for a comprehensive overview, see the papers by Fonagy and Hesse and Main (this issue).

The Practice of Infant Observation

INFANT OBSERVATION, AS INSTITUTED IN THE CHILD PSYCHOTHERAPY training at the Tavistock by Esther Bick, is a discipline that develops the intellectual and emotional muscle of the observer. The practice is this: every week, by carefully negotiated prearrangement, a trainee visits a family at a regular time to observe a baby in the context of its family. There is usually at least one preliminary visit before the baby is born; after the birth, the observations begin as soon as possible and continue until the child is 2 years old. The observer has to find a place in the family: friendly, but neutral, he or she must discover by trial and error a way in which to watch the baby growing up in the family context. Avoiding, on one hand, premature intimacy and the perils of intrusiveness and, on the other, the danger of being thought chilly and unhelpful can be a difficult task. Observers are there by courtesy of the families, and if parents—perhaps especially mothers in the earliest weeks—are often glad to find someone as interested in the babies as they are they are themselves, it is always up to observers to remember that they are there to learn.

The learning experience can prove to be a formative one. Each observation lasts an hour, and after the hour the observer leaves to write up as soon as possible a detailed account of the observation.

MARY AINSWORTH WAS A LIVELY, PHYSICALLY ROBUST WOMAN. She had a notable liking for parties, dancing, books, music, whiskey, tennis, bridge, crossword puzzles, basketball, board games, geography, and meteorology. On entrance to her home in Charlottesville, where she took up residence in 1973, a visitor would note immediately that (as in the case of her previous home in Baltimore) it was neat. pretty, and well-cared for, and was backed by a wide screened porch where she spent much time. Her house was filled with comfortable, silk-covered chairs and sofas, oriental carpets, and Herman Maril paintings, which she collected. The overflow of serious books and papers was confined to her study, which also contained a tall bookcase full of paper-back murder mysteries. Like John Bowlby, she believed that at least 6- to 8-week yearly holidays were a good thing, and she took seaside holidays of this duration. By the 1980's she began to complain that academics in general were gradually growing too invested in grant-getting and publications, as indicated by the ever-diminishing number of dinner parties. In the years in which I knew her, she was well-groomed, well-dressed, and liked oright colors, and this is partially attributable to a long, personal psychoanalysis which I discuss below.

Margot Waddell   Consultant Child Psychotherapist, Adolescent Department, Tavistock Clinic, and associate member, British Psycho-Analytical Society

EXPLORING ADOLESCENT DIFFICULTIES WITH A VIEW to possible therapeutic treatment involves attempting to engage a troubled, and often confused, individual in beginning to think, to think in a very specific and probably unfamiliar way. Beginning to think can itself be a frightening process. It necessitates learning about oneself. “They' all hate learning,” says the Psychoanalyst in Bion's (1979) final Memoir. “It makes them develop—swell up” (p.8)—pregnant, that is, with a new idea, a new birth/thought in the mind.

It is often at adolescence that the issue of different kinds of learning and thinking and their implications for development take on some kind of clarity. The emotional ferment stirred up by puberty and its complex aftermath is one that adolescents find themselves alarmingly, and often unexpectedly, caught up in. Inner conflicts and anxieties are aroused, which many seek to avoid, if at all possible. Some seem to stop thinking independently altogether and submerge themselves either in the shared mentality of group life, and/or in activities that are literally mindless, such as drugs, alcohol, or substance abuse. At the other extreme, some may try to rely on intelligence itself as a defense against facing and thinking about turbulent and often contradictory feelings—as a way of avoiding intimacy and evading engagement with “the agitation of inexperience” (Copley, 1993).
